Mine wasn't that utilitarian in an economic sense, my grandparents are Portuguese and don't speak English so I wanted to learn Portuguese in order to finally have a conversation with them without my dad translating. Portuguese hasn't helped me in my career at all, I work in the live music industry in the US, but it has been an incredibly fulfilling skill for my life. Being able to speak to my family without help has been amazing, and I'm able to follow the news in Portugal much better. I do struggle to understand Brazilians though because of how different the accent and vocabulary is, and most of the Portuguese-speakers I encounter in my day to day life in the USA are Brazilians, but I'm still glad I picked the European dialect specifically because it's much more personally fulfilling.

text:
I'm an honors student, and the first thing I'd advise you to do is reach out to the Honors program and ask them what their specific honors program entails. Some universities really do have honors programs that are just extra work. My school isn't like that.

At upper level honors, I'm designing my own research projects and finding professors willing to oversee and grade them for me. I'll soon have a team of three professors from my department overlooking my research, since that's the next step. I get to study what's interesting to me, and I get one-on-one mentorship from my professors, which is a lot more beneficial than being one of 20ish people in a class. Feedback is more detailed, I have more time to ask questions, and since I'm picking the topics, I get to stick to what I really want to study for the rest of my life.

For me, I'm interested in pursuing college all the way up to a PhD, which means I want my academic record to be as good as possible when I apply to graduate schools next year. It also means that I'm pursuing a career path where the skills I'm learning will be important to me long-term. If you also intend on going to grad school, I'd say it's worth it.

The last thing I would add is that for a lot of students, honors can be great socially. My uni does honors-only dorms, honors social events, and I even get paid for volunteering to table certain events for the honors society. A lot of students, especially STEM students, can get hefty research grants for summer projects at my school too.

TL:DR; Reach out to your school's honors society. Ask them what the expectations for the program are, and what benefits are offered. Then consider if you can/want to consistently meet those expectations, and if the benefits sound worthwhile to you.

Do you mean like US Federal Work Study? Federal work study supervisor here! Students work an hourly wage at their job. Once the student hits their work study award amount (paid by federal student aid), the student either stops working or the department they work for starts footing the bill. Depebding how your insistution organized things, your award may work out to something like 10 hr/wk.

When I was a student, I really wish someone explained it more to me. It is a great program that students should take advantage of. Work Study students have more restrictions than hourly employees, but it's common sense things like not working during class time and making sure your supervisor sets expectations. But, you get the experience of a part time job with flexibility around your class schedule.
